messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Psychiatrist
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 37

She is 58, a psychiatrist who has spent most of her adult life listening carefully for the shape of other people’s fear, but when she tells her own story, she does it in fragments at first. She is a divorced woman from Oceania, practical and articulate, the kind of person who has always been the steady one in the room. Before the accident, her days are orderly and full. She works long hours, moves between inpatient reviews and outpatient sessions, writes notes late into the evening, and prides herself on staying calm under pressure. She has built a life around competence. She has learned, over years of practice, how to sit with suffering without being overwhelmed by it.

The accident happens on an ordinary weekday, which is part of what still unsettles her. She is driving home after work in heavy rain, tired but not distracted, thinking about a patient she has seen that afternoon. At an intersection, another vehicle runs through at speed. She remembers the impossible brightness of headlights where they should not be, then the violent crush of impact into the side of her car. Metal folds. Glass explodes inward. For a moment she cannot tell what part of her body is still attached to the seat and what has been thrown sideways. She smells petrol and wet upholstery. Her first thought is not coherent fear but a sharp, clinical assessment: This may be fatal. She is trapped, unable to open the door, and she can hear a strange sound before realizing it is her own voice making small, involuntary noises. She thinks the car might catch fire. She thinks she is about to die alone in traffic.

She survives with injuries that heal more quickly than she expects her mind to. In the hospital she is composed, even faintly embarrassed by the attention. She answers questions efficiently. She minimizes. Visitors tell her how lucky she is. She repeats it back to them—I was lucky—because it is true, and because it seems to close the conversation. But once she is home, luck does not feel like the right word. Sleep changes first. Each time she begins to drift off, her body jolts awake with the sensation of impact. She sees the headlights again, vivid and immediate, as if they are entering the room. Sometimes she wakes with her heart pounding and the sheets damp beneath her, already braced for something catastrophic.

She returns to work before she feels ready because staying home makes her feel brittle and exposed. In her consulting room she can still ask measured questions, still keep time, still formulate. To colleagues she appears intact. But the effort of seeming normal consumes her. She startles at sounds she used to ignore—the slam of a door in the corridor, a trolley rattling too quickly over uneven flooring. When an ambulance siren rises outside the clinic, her chest tightens and she loses the thread of what a patient is saying. She begins positioning herself near exits without quite meaning to. In traffic she grips the steering wheel until her hands ache. She avoids the intersection where the crash happened, then gradually avoids driving in rain, at night, on busy roads, and eventually anywhere unfamiliar. She tells herself these are reasonable precautions, but her world starts to narrow around them.

What troubles her most is the intrusion of the accident into places she considers professionally sacred. A patient describes a motor vehicle collision, and she feels an electric flash through her body before her mind catches up. She becomes acutely aware of her breathing, of the room, of the need not to show it. Afterwards she sits alone in her office, ashamed of how close she has come to losing her composure. She has spent decades helping others name avoidance, hypervigilance, re-experiencing; now she notices herself using longer routes, scanning rearview mirrors, checking and rechecking that doors are locked, hesitating before turning the ignition. This recognition does not protect her from it. If anything, it deepens the humiliation. She thinks, with some bitterness, that insight is not the same as control.

At home, evenings are the hardest. Since her divorce, she has lived alone and once enjoyed the quiet. Now silence feels too permeable, as though danger can enter it without warning. She leaves the television on for company she does not really want. Friends invite her out, and she often declines, saying she is tired from work. It is easier than explaining why restaurants near busy roads make her feel trapped, or why she studies weather forecasts with disproportionate concern. She notices herself becoming less patient, more withdrawn. Small inconveniences provoke tears or anger that surprise her. She used to read before bed; now she scrolls aimlessly, delaying sleep.

Months later, she still measures time against the accident: before the impact, after the impact. She knows she is functioning. She is still seeing patients, paying bills, answering messages, showing up. But she no longer moves through the world with the unconscious trust she once had. Ordinary travel carries a sense of threat. Rest feels conditional. Her body behaves as though the collision has not fully ended, as though some part of her remains inside the wrecked car, waiting for the next sound of twisting metal and the next burst of light.
